title: Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families
one_liner: A flat-fee, advocate-supervised 'estate file' service that gets a dead parent's or grandfather's land, shares and dormant accounts legally transferred, sold to the adult children who pay from Nairobi, Dallas or Dubai.
customer: Salaried urban and diaspora Kenyans aged 30-55 whose rural parents or grandparents died (or are old) with land still registered in a dead person's name. They pay from abroad or from the city. A secondary B2B payer is any SACCO, coop or bank that needs cleared successions before it releases deposits or lends against land.
problem: Most rural family land is still titled to a dead grandfather or father because nobody completed succession. The process needs a chief's letter, a death certificate, consents from every heir, gazettement, a wait before confirmation of grant, and then transmission at the land registry, which is often 1-3 years and many trips. Until it is done the land cannot be leased, mortgaged, subdivided or cleanly sold, siblings fight, and the deceased's SACCO deposits, coop shares, insurance and pension sit unclaimed. The real blocker is coordinating 8 to 20 relatives to sign, not the court.
solution: Wedge product is a 'Family Estate Map' for roughly KES 15-25k (pricing to be tested). The child sends photos of the title, IDs, death certificate and old share certificates over WhatsApp. An LLM pipeline extracts names and parcel numbers, handles the multiple-name and spelling-variant problem in Kenyan naming, builds the family tree and likely heirs, and lists the consents needed. It runs official land searches and asset-discovery letters to SACCOs, coops, insurers and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, then outputs a court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits. A home-county field agent collects the chief's letter and relatives' signatures or thumbprints, with video proof of consent. Partner advocates then file and shepherd the case at their own scale fees. Later upsells are surveyor subdivision and lease or loan readiness.
why_now: The generation that took up land in the 1960s-80s through settlement schemes and land-buying companies is dying now, so the succession backlog is peaking. Diaspora remittances are near record levels (roughly US$5bn a year), and families increasingly ask 'sort out the land' rather than 'build a house'. Digitised land records (Ardhisasa) and court e-filing reduce physical running, though their current coverage needs checking. LLMs can now read messy scanned title and ID documents and draft forms in English while chatting with clients in Swahili. I could not run live searches, so verify current UFAA agent rules, court e-filing scope for successions, and fee schedules before building.
revenue_model: Flat fee per estate file, paid by M-Pesa or card from abroad. Advocate fees are billed by the advocates themselves, so the company sells software and case management and does not split fees with non-lawyers. Asset discovery is a flat add-on fee, not a percentage cut of UFAA payouts, because UFAA discourages middlemen taking a share. B2B revenue is per cleaned member estate from SACCOs and coops. Later there is referral income from surveyors and land-backed lenders once titles are clean.
non_obvious_insight: Rural Kenya's biggest pool of unused collateral is land trapped in the name of the dead. The bottleneck is family coordination and evidence gathering, so the product is a coordination workflow sold to the sibling who has money and guilt, not a land registry or a lawyer marketplace. VCs looking at land-tech miss that the payer is the diaspora child, not the farmer.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Murang'a or Kakamega) and recruit two advocates who already do succession work. Build intake on WhatsApp Business, Airtable and an LLM extraction script. Sell 10 files at a pilot discount through your own family network, church and alumni groups, and diaspora WhatsApp and Facebook groups such as Kenyans in Texas or the UK. Publish a free 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' checker as lead-gen. Track days from intake to gazettement as the core metric.

tournament.cluster: Diaspora families managing death, care and property across borders
judge_notes: operator: rank 5/25 - Original, large backlog, payer is guilty diaspora child; warm-network first sales, but thin unit economics.
contrarian: rank 4/25 - Payer is diaspora child, not farmer; VCs miss it; coordination workflow on huge trapped-land pool.
vc: rank 1/25 - Huge trapped-asset pain, unusual payer (diaspora child), non-obvious, replicable across Africa and South Asia; coordination workflow is the moat.

competitors.name: Luru (open-source 'Kenya's Digital Succession Copilot')
competitors.what_they_do: Hobbyist NestJS/React app that scores succession readiness, builds family trees, does estate inventory and checks Cap 160 (Law of Succession Act) compliance. It is software only, with no field agents, consent collection, advocates or asset-discovery letters. I could not read its README because the repo is not in this session's allowed list. My description comes from the search-result blurb.
competitors.scale_or_funding: 0 stars, 0 forks, created Sept 2025, no funding signal

competitors.name: Wakili-Intel (AI drafting copilot for Kenyan advocates)
competitors.what_they_do: Open-source AI copilot that researches Kenya Law and drafts pleadings for advocates. It is a possible substitute for the document-drafting step of the idea, but it does no client intake, heir mapping or field work.
competitors.scale_or_funding: 0 stars, created July 2026, hobby or hackathon project

competitors.name: Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority (UFAA)
competitors.what_they_do: Government register of unclaimed assets. Beneficiary claims for a deceased owner use Form 4B and require a Certificate of Confirmation of Grant from the High Court or a Certificate of Summary Administration from the Public Trustee. Agent claims (Form 4D) are allowed only for living owners and need a registered power of attorney. It is an incumbent channel for the asset-discovery piece, not a competitor for the whole bundle.
competitors.scale_or_funding: State agency, free to use as far as I could see. The FAQ pages I fetched say nothing about fees or intermediaries either way.

competitors.name: Ardhisasa (Ministry of Lands digital land registry)
competitors.what_they_do: Government online land registry for searches and dealings. It is the system of record the idea depends on, and a possible future incumbent if it adds guided succession or transmission workflows. The fetch returned only the site name, so I could not confirm which services or counties it covers, or whether transmission by succession runs end-to-end there.

competitors.name: Kenya Judiciary e-filing / Case Tracking System
competitors.what_they_do: Court e-filing portal used by advocates. My recollection, unverified, is that it accepts succession causes. The URL returned HTTP 503 when I fetched it. It lowers the cost of filing but does nothing about heir coordination.

competitors.url: n/a - could not be verified because the web search budget ran out
competitors.what_they_do: Advocates already file successions for clients, and some serve diaspora clients over WhatsApp or email. They are the real incumbent substitute. None of them was checked for a productised, flat-fee, consent-collecting offer, and I did not confirm any funded startup doing this.

competition.white_space: Provisional, because the web search budget hit its 200-call cap before any search returned results. My evidence comes only from direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches. I found no funded startup, product or open-source project that combines (a) diaspora-paid flat-fee intake, (b) heir mapping across Kenyan name variants, (c) field-agent collection of chief's letters and thumbprint or video consent from 8-20 relatives, and (d) hand-off to partner advocates. The software pieces (family tree, readiness score, drafting copilots) exist only as zero-star hobby repos. Government platforms (Ardhisasa, court e-filing, UFAA) cover filing and claiming but not multi-heir coordination. UFAA's beneficiary claim rule makes succession a prerequisite for claiming a dead person's unclaimed assets, so a succession-first product that unlocks those assets has a logical hook. The unserved wedge is the coordination and evidence-gathering layer sold to the paying sibling abroad. It is still unproven whether ordinary advocates or land-buying-company agents already do this informally, because I could not search for them.
competition.evidence_of_demand: Thin and mostly structural. I could not run the searches for forum complaints, press coverage, RFPs or spend on workarounds. (1) UFAA requires a Certificate of Confirmation of Grant (High Court) or a Public Trustee summary administration certificate before beneficiaries can claim a deceased person's unclaimed assets, and beneficiary claims take up to 90 days versus 30 for owners: https://www.ufaa.go.ke/claiming-instructions/ and https://www.ufaa.go.ke/faqs/. This confirms that succession gates asset release. (2) Several open-source Kenyan succession and legal-AI projects exist, which shows builder interest: https://github.com/CoolCerebralTech/luru and https://github.com/fab679/wakili-intel. That is not evidence of customers paying. Not verified: the size of the 'land in a dead person's name' backlog, diaspora willingness to pay KES 15-25k, and the idea's ~US$5bn remittance figure. From memory, the remittance figure is about right and the backlog is widely reported. The idea's claim that UFAA 'discourages middlemen taking a share' was not confirmed on the UFAA pages I fetched, which say nothing about fees or intermediaries.
competition.sharper_angle: (1) Fix the legal structure first. From memory, and it must be verified with a Kenyan advocate, the Advocates Act restricts non-advocates from preparing court documents or conveyancing instruments for a fee. Selling a 'court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits' from a non-lawyer company is the main structural risk. Make a partner law firm the contracting entity of record, or sell only the non-legal layer (heir map, name-variant reconciliation, official searches, consent and thumbprint capture with video proof). The advocate then bills for the filing. (2) Sell the coordination layer, not the paperwork: a 'Family Consent Ledger' that gets 8-20 heirs to sign and tracks days from intake to gazettement. That avoids competing with advocates and with Ardhisasa or e-filing. (3) Start with cohorts that share one registry and chief: members of the same 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county. Batch searches and field trips give better unit economics than single estates. (4) Keep the SACCO and coop B2B lane as a second channel, sold as cleared-estate throughput. (5) Treat asset discovery as a flat add-on, since UFAA claims need a confirmed grant first. That makes it an upsell after succession, not a lead product. (6) Before building, do the searches I could not run: Kenyan legal-tech startups, land-buying-company succession help desks, diaspora land-services firms, and whether Ardhisasa handles transmission by succession end-to-end.
